items.title: Meta is increasingly positioning itself to challenge Apple’s dominance in consumer technology as AI changes how users interact with hardware
items.content_excerpt: Meta is increasingly positioning itself to challenge Apple’s dominance in consumer technology as AI changes how users interact with hardware. Mark Zuckerberg’s recent announcements around Muse, Meta’s AI assistant, suggest the company is pursuing a broader hardware strategy that could compete with Apple’s iPhone-centered ecosystem. According to Needham analyst Laura Martin, Meta is “developing products that directly attack” Apple’s core business. The strategy goes beyond software, with Meta exploring AI-powered devices that could eventually become a new interface between consumers and digital services. The broader bet is that AI assistants and purpose-built hardware could reduce the central role smartphones currently play. Apple’s iPhone remains the foundation of its consumer ecosystem, while Meta is attempting to use its AI capabilities and hardware portfolio to establish a different model for the AI era. $META $AAPL

items.title: Software stocks staged a major comeback in the third quarter as fears that AI would disrupt traditional software businesses eased, making th
items.content_excerpt: Software stocks staged a major comeback in the third quarter as fears that AI would disrupt traditional software businesses eased, making the sector one of the market’s strongest areas. The iShares Expanded Tech-Software ETF rose 17% during the quarter, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF fell 11%, highlighting the rotation away from some high-flying chip stocks. Salesforce surged 46% as investors increasingly viewed AI as a growth opportunity, helped by its Claude integration through “Claudeforce,” strong quarterly results and share buybacks. Jim Cramer said Salesforce still has room to climb and was similarly bullish on Microsoft, which gained 37%, citing strong Copilot demand, accelerating Azure growth and signs that its data-center investments are starting to generate returns. Workday and Veeva jumped 55% and 60%, respectively, while CrowdStrike gained 39% as AI-driven cyber threats reinforced demand for security. $CRM $MSFT $WDAY $VEEV $CRWD

items.content_excerpt: $AVGO The $42B headline needs much more precision. It is up to $42B of financing capacity — not $42B already lent by Broadcom and not $42B of immediate credit exposure. Broadcom can use a financing partner, the debt can potentially convert into Anthropic equity, and Anthropic has already placed cash in a restricted account for Broadcom’s benefit, with provisions requiring additional contributions. Even more important: certain defaults can make a substantial portion of Anthropic’s lease obligations immediately due while restricting further draws on the financing facility. That is a very different risk profile from “Broadcom loaned Anthropic $42B.”

items.title: Rocket Lab announced a multiyear agreement with Synspective covering 20 Electron launches, its largest commercial launch contract to date. T
items.content_excerpt: Rocket Lab announced a multiyear agreement with Synspective covering 20 Electron launches, its largest commercial launch contract to date. The deal calls for Rocket Lab to launch 20 StriX synthetic-aperture radar satellites into sun-synchronous orbit from Launch Complex 1 between 2028 and 2031. Financial terms were not disclosed. The agreement brings the total number of Electron missions contracted by Synspective to 47, making the Tokyo-based Earth-observation company Rocket Lab’s largest launch customer. Synspective said Electron’s precision and reliability have been critical to scaling its StriX satellite constellation, while the 20 dedicated launches provide greater certainty for its long-term expansion. Rocket Lab CEO Peter Beck described the deal as a vote of confidence in Electron’s launch cadence, mission reliability and orbital accuracy. $RKLB

items.title: $UVIX This won’t spike until some random, unforeseen event comes out of nowhere. I was long a load of UVIX/VIX calls in 2024. Trump got shot
items.content_excerpt: $UVIX This won’t spike until some random, unforeseen event comes out of nowhere. I was long a load of UVIX/VIX calls in 2024. Trump got shot and various other things happened that you’d expect to spike vol — yet VIX spent ages around 12–13 and my options just bled. Literally the day after they expired, we got the bad jobs number and the yen carry-trade unwind and VIX exploded. Luckily I shorted vol into that spike, and within about a week VIX had almost completely retraced. Lesson I learned: it’s a hell of a lot easier to short a vol spike than sit there bleeding premium waiting for the event that finally causes one. Trading something like UVIX has its own version of “theta” through futures contango and the constant daily reset/decay. It’s not exactly the same as option theta, but the end result can feel pretty similar — time is working against you while you wait for the move. I’ll trade it long tactically, but I wouldn’t want to sit long this stuff for any length of time.$SPY

items.title: $UBER Global chemical manufacturer Oxea needed a logistics partner that would go beyond managing transportation by region but as one global
items.content_excerpt: $UBER Global chemical manufacturer Oxea needed a logistics partner that would go beyond managing transportation by region but as one global network. The company selected Uber Freight, which will provide more than outsourced transportation management by handling day-to-day transportation across truckload, rail and ocean, according to a Sept. 15 press release. The logistics company will handle the company’s logistics network that spans the U.S., Canada, Mexico and Europe. “Managing chemical logistics is complex, as moving products requires specialized equipment and handling, documentation, and coordination among plants, carriers and customers, per the release. Managing those components as one network makes it easier for Uber Freight to have a clearer view of what is happening across Oxea’s network, and make adjustments as needed. Oxea aims to anticipate issues sooner and respond faster, Oxea’s Chief Supply Chain Officer Scott Farmer said in the release.”

items.title: $BP $XOM Wells Fargo made it a pair trade: upgraded BP to Overweight from Equal Weight and raised the target to 57 from 48, while cutting Ex
items.content_excerpt: $BP $XOM Wells Fargo made it a pair trade: upgraded BP to Overweight from Equal Weight and raised the target to 57 from 48, while cutting Exxon to Equal Weight from Overweight with its 182 target unchanged. The tell is in the asymmetry. Wells Fargo did not lower its view of Exxon, it changed its preference. Analyst Sam Margolin argues BP's 2027 EV/EBITDA multiple is nearly half that of its US peers, and that gap has historically preceded BP outperformance. The mechanism is the balance sheet. Wells Fargo expects commodity and trading conditions to pull forward BP's 14 billion debt target, and sees financial debt dropping to about 6.2 billion by the end of 2026 on Castrol sale proceeds plus cash flow. BP added about 1.1% Thursday. The test is the deleveraging arriving on schedule.

items.title: President Donald Trump said Wednesday he is still considering a ban on U.S. diesel exports to ease elevated energy prices, but acknowledged
items.content_excerpt: President Donald Trump said Wednesday he is still considering a ban on U.S. diesel exports to ease elevated energy prices, but acknowledged the measure could have a “negative impact” on gasoline prices. His comments appeared less supportive than three days earlier, when he said he was “very seriously” considering the move. Trump said an export ban could lower diesel prices but potentially raise gasoline and other costs. He also pointed to a recent recovery in crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, saying oil prices could begin to decline as flows return to prewar levels. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said diesel prices have fallen over the past week and could decline further, although supplies remain tight because of disruptions linked to conflicts in Russia and the Middle East, as well as reduced Chinese exports. He said U.S. refiners are operating at record levels and additional European supplies could help ease the market. $XOM $SHEL $CVX

items.title: $OXY Goldman is the first big bank to actually upgrade the rating this month, not just lift the target. Neil Mehta took Occidental to Buy fr
items.content_excerpt: $OXY Goldman is the first big bank to actually upgrade the rating this month, not just lift the target. Neil Mehta took Occidental to Buy from Neutral late Wednesday, target to 69 from 63. About 25% upside. UBS, Wells Fargo and Evercore all raised targets in September without touching their ratings. The pitch is not the oil price. It is the balance sheet and the 4 billion of annual sustainable cash flow management says it can reach by 2030, with 85% of it structural enough to hold at lower prices. The part already done: OXY cut principal debt 1.9 billion in Q2 alone, to 11.8 billion, the lowest since 2019. The annualized interest bill is down about 630 million from 2025 levels. Cash that stops leaving the business every year regardless of the barrel. The wrinkle: OXY runs with essentially no commodity hedges. Every dollar of oil price flows straight to cash flow. With Brent back over 100, that is the upside. The downside is exactly as exposed. Shares rose 4.4% Thursday.

items.title: $BA small continuation helicopter contract ; Today’s announcement is the first full-rate production order for the MH-139A Grey Wolf, the sam
items.content_excerpt: $BA small continuation helicopter contract ; Today’s announcement is the first full-rate production order for the MH-139A Grey Wolf, the same Air Force Huey-replacement program from 2018. Boeing said on October 1 that the Air Force ordered four more MH-139A Grey Wolf helicopters. Military Times, citing a Boeing spokesperson, puts the value at roughly $85 million, including some sustainment work. The award date was September 25; Boeing announced it today. Deliveries are expected in 2028 or 2029. That brings the total under contract to 42, of which Boeing has delivered 27. Six of the earlier aircraft were test airframes. The Air Force declared initial operating capability earlier this year, so this is the first lot under full-rate production rather than low-rate initial production. Context on the larger program: the 2018 award was a ceiling of $2.38 billion for up to 84 helicopters, delivered through 2032, to replace UH-1N Hueys that guard the nuclear missile fields. In 2024 the Air Force cut the planned buy to 42, which triggered a Nunn-McCurdy cost breach. Budget documents later raised the objective to 56 aircraft, so this lot does not finish the program. The Grey Wolf is Boeing’s militarized version of Leonardo’s AW139, used for missile-field security and transport of security forces. Part if 2.38 billion contract ratified and continuing Company-wide backlog was a record $715 billion, but commercial airplanes are about $597 billion of that. Defense is the $85 billion piece. • This week’s awards — the Grey Wolf lot, the $2.38 billion F-15EX order, and the F/A-XX development contract — are not in the June 30 figure. Third-quarter results are not out yet. items.content_excerpt: President Donald Trump said Wednesday he is still considering a ban on U.S. diesel exports to ease elevated energy prices, but acknowledged the measure could have a “negative impact” on gasoline prices. His comments appeared less supportive than three days earlier, when he said he was “very seriously” considering the move. Trump said an export ban could lower diesel prices but potentially raise gasoline and other costs. He also pointed to a recent recovery in crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, saying oil prices could begin to decline as flows return to prewar levels. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said diesel prices have fallen over the past week and could decline further, although supplies remain tight because of disruptions linked to conflicts in Russia and the Middle East, as well as reduced Chinese exports. He said U.S. refiners are operating at record levels and additional European supplies could help ease the market. $XOM $SHEL $CVX

$UVIX This won’t spike until some random, unforeseen event comes out of nowhere. I was long a load of UVIX/VIX calls in 2024. Trump got shot and various other things happened that you’d expect to spike vol — yet VIX spent ages around 12–13 and my options just bled. Literally the day after they expired, we got the bad jobs number and the yen carry-trade unwind and VIX exploded. Luckily I shorted vol into that spike, and within about a week VIX had almost completely retraced. Lesson I learned: it’s a hell of a lot easier to short a vol spike than sit there bleeding premium waiting for the event that finally causes one. Trading something like UVIX has its own version of “theta” through futures contango and the constant daily reset/decay. It’s not exactly the same as option theta, but the end result can feel pretty similar — time is working against you while you wait for the move. I’ll trade it long tactically, but I wouldn’t want to sit long this stuff for any length of time.$SPY

messages.body: $OXY Goldman is the first big bank to actually upgrade the rating this month, not just lift the target. Neil Mehta took Occidental to Buy from Neutral late Wednesday, target to 69 from 63. About 25% upside. UBS, Wells Fargo and Evercore all raised targets in September without touching their ratings. The pitch is not the oil price. It is the balance sheet and the 4 billion of annual sustainable cash flow management says it can reach by 2030, with 85% of it structural enough to hold at lower prices. The part already done: OXY cut principal debt 1.9 billion in Q2 alone, to 11.8 billion, the lowest since 2019. The annualized interest bill is down about 630 million from 2025 levels. Cash that stops leaving the business every year regardless of the barrel. The wrinkle: OXY runs with essentially no commodity hedges. Every dollar of oil price flows straight to cash flow. With Brent back over 100, that is the upside. The downside is exactly as exposed. Shares rose 4.4% Thursday.

Boeing said on October 1 that the Air Force ordered four more MH-139A Grey Wolf helicopters. Military Times, citing a Boeing spokesperson, puts the value at roughly $85 million, including some sustainment work. The award date was September 25; Boeing announced it today. Deliveries are expected in 2028 or 2029. That brings the total under contract to 42, of which Boeing has delivered 27. Six of the earlier aircraft were test airframes. The Air Force declared initial operating capability earlier this year, so this is the first lot under full-rate production rather than low-rate initial production. Context on the larger program: the 2018 award was a ceiling of $2.38 billion for up to 84 helicopters, delivered through 2032, to replace UH-1N Hueys that guard the nuclear missile fields. In 2024 the Air Force cut the planned buy to 42, which triggered a Nunn-McCurdy cost breach. Budget documents later raised the objective to 56 aircraft, so this lot does not finish the program. The Grey Wolf is Boeing’s militarized version of Leonardo’s AW139, used for missile-field security and transport of security forces.
